title: Stop writing long null checks
note: Optional chaining stops at null/undefined. ?? only falls back on null/undefined, so 0 and "" survive.
caption: Optional chaining + nullish coalescing replace a whole chain of && checks. Bonus: ?? won't throw away valid falsy values like 0 or an empty string.

title: Deep copy without JSON hacks
note: structuredClone is built into browsers and Node 17+. No lodash needed.
caption: JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj)) silently breaks Dates, Maps, Sets and undefined. structuredClone handles them properly.

title: Get the last item the clean way
code:
const items = [10, 20, 30];

items[items.length - 1]; // 30
items.at(-1);             // 30
items.at(-2);             // 20
note: Array.prototype.at() accepts negative indexes. Works on strings too.
caption: Small one, but it reads so much better. .at(-1) gives you the last element without the length math.

title: Your awaits might be slow for no reason
note: If two requests don't depend on each other, start them together.
caption: Back-to-back awaits run one after another. When the calls are independent, Promise.all runs them at the same time and cuts the wait.

title: Group arrays in one line
note: Native Object.groupBy. Supported in all modern browsers and Node 21+.
caption: No more reduce() boilerplate to group data. Object.groupBy is now built into the language.

title: Stop firing an API call on every keystroke
note: The search only runs once the user pauses typing.
caption: A search box that calls the API on every keystroke wastes requests and can show results out of order. Debounce it.

title: The event loop in one picture
note: Promises and queueMicrotask always run before the next setTimeout, even setTimeout(fn, 0). That's why a resolved promise logs before a zero-delay timer.
caption: The call stack clears, then ALL queued microtasks run, then one macrotask (like a timer or I/O callback) runs. Mixing these up causes some of the gnarliest async bugs.

title: Closures vs. memory leaks

left.label: Leaky
left.body: A closure captures a huge array just to read one field from it. The whole array stays alive as long as the closure does.

right.label: Fixed
right.body: Extract only the value you need before creating the closure. The large object can then be garbage collected.

note: Closures keep their entire outer scope alive, not just the variables you use. In long-running apps that adds up.
caption: A closure doesn't just remember the variable you reference — it keeps the whole enclosing scope reachable. In long-lived listeners or timers, that's a classic memory leak source.

title: Use satisfies, not type annotations
note: satisfies checks the shape but keeps the exact inferred type.
caption: Annotating with : Theme widens your object and you lose autocomplete on keys. satisfies validates it and keeps the precise type.

title: Turn arrays into union types
note: One source of truth for runtime values and types.
caption: Define your options once with as const, then derive the type from it. Add a role to the array and the type updates automatically.

title: Narrow types without a library
note: catch clauses are typed unknown. A type predicate narrows it safely.
caption: e.message on a catch variable is a type error in strict mode because catch values are unknown. A small type guard fixes it without any casts.

title: Never use index as a key
note: Index keys make React reuse the wrong component state after sorts or deletes.
caption: If inputs in your list start showing the wrong values after deleting an item, check your keys. Use a stable id, not the array index.

title: You don't need useEffect for this
note: If a value can be calculated from props or state, calculate it during render.
caption: Syncing derived values with useEffect causes an extra render and bugs. Compute it directly instead.

title: The setState bug that hides in plain sight
note: Use the updater function when new state depends on the previous state.
caption: count is a snapshot from the current render. The updater form always gets the latest value.

title: Expensive initial state? Make it lazy
note: Pass a function to useState and React only calls it on the first render.
caption: A tiny change that can save real work on every re-render: pass an initializer function instead of the computed value.

title: useMemo vs useCallback, pick right

left.label: useMemo
left.body: Caches a computed VALUE between renders. Use it for expensive calculations like filtering a big list.

right.label: useCallback
right.body: Caches a FUNCTION reference between renders. Use it so child components don't re-render from a new prop identity.

note: useCallback(fn, deps) is really just useMemo(() => fn, deps) under the hood.
caption: Both exist to stop unnecessary work, but they cache different things. Reaching for the wrong one is a common React code review comment.

title: Fetch data directly in Server Components
note: No useEffect, no loading spinner flash, and the data never ships as client JS.
caption: In the Next.js App Router, components are server components by default. You can make them async and fetch right inside.

title: Dynamic SEO titles per page
note: Each dynamic route gets its own title, description and OG tags.
caption: Every blog post or product page sharing one generic title hurts SEO. generateMetadata gives each route its own.

title: Forms without an API route
note: Server Actions run on the server. Always validate input inside them.
caption: With Server Actions, a form can call a server function directly. Less boilerplate than writing a separate API route.

title: Responsive font size, zero media queries
note: The heading scales with the viewport but never goes below or above your limits.
caption: clamp() gives you fluid typography in one line. No more stacking breakpoints just for font sizes.

title: CSS finally has a parent selector
note: :has() is supported in all modern browsers.
caption: Things that used to need JavaScript, like styling a parent based on its children, now work in pure CSS.

title: Components that respond to their container
note: The card adapts to the space it gets, not the whole screen width.
caption: Media queries look at the viewport. Container queries look at the parent, which is what reusable components actually need.

title: Specificity: the part everyone skips
note: One class selector always outranks any number of element/tag selectors. An id (1,0,0) beats any number of classes. !important beats all of it and should be avoided.
caption: CSS specificity is a 4-part score: inline styles, ids, classes/attributes/pseudo-classes, then elements. More specific always wins, no matter the order in the file.

title: Scroll-linked zoom effect with GSAP
note: scrub ties the animation progress to the scrollbar position.
caption: The classic zoom-on-scroll hero effect. scrub: true makes it follow your scroll instead of playing once.

title: Use GSAP in React without memory leaks
note: useGSAP scopes selectors to the ref and reverts animations on unmount.
caption: Running GSAP inside a plain useEffect often leaves animations behind when components unmount. The official useGSAP hook cleans up for you.

title: Add a timeout to fetch in one line
note: Works in Node 18+ and all modern browsers.
caption: fetch has no timeout by default, so a slow server can hang your request forever. AbortSignal.timeout fixes that.

title: You may not need nodemon anymore
code:
# restarts on file changes
node --watch server.js

# load .env without dotenv
node --env-file=.env server.js
note: Both flags are built into modern Node versions.
caption: Two dev dependencies you can often drop: nodemon and dotenv. Node does both natively now.

title: Single-threaded, but not what you think
note: Your JS code runs on one thread, but Node offloads file I/O, DNS and crypto to a libuv thread pool (4 threads by default) so the main thread isn't blocked.
caption: "Node is single-threaded" is only half true. The event loop is single-threaded, but heavy I/O work happens on background threads you never see. That's why Node handles thousands of connections fine but chokes on CPU-bound loops.

title: Cache invalidation, the two options

left.label: TTL expiry
left.body: Simple: set a time limit and let the cache go stale automatically. Risk: users can see outdated data until it expires.

right.label: Explicit invalidation
right.body: Accurate: delete or update the cache entry the moment the source data changes. Risk: easy to miss a code path and leave stale entries.

note: Most production systems use both: a short TTL as a safety net plus explicit invalidation for the common update paths.
caption: "There are only two hard things in computer science: cache invalidation and naming things." Here's the actual tradeoff behind that joke.

title: Why rate limiting uses token buckets
note: Allows short bursts up to the bucket size while still enforcing a steady average rate.
caption: A fixed-window counter resets unfairly at the boundary and allows 2x the limit right at the edge. Token bucket smooths that out and still allows bursts.

title: Find out why your query is slow
note: A sequential scan on a big table usually means a missing index.
caption: Don't guess at SQL performance. EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows exactly how Postgres runs your query.

title: An index can make writes slower
note: Each index on a table has to be updated on every insert/update/delete. 10 indexes on a write-heavy table means 10x the index maintenance work per write.
caption: Indexes aren't free. They speed up reads but slow down writes, since the database has to maintain every index's structure on each change. Index what you actually query, not everything.

title: SQL vs NoSQL isn't the real question

left.label: Relational (SQL)
left.body: Strong consistency, joins, and schema enforcement. Best when relationships between data matter and correctness is critical.

right.label: Document (NoSQL)
right.body: Flexible schema, fast at scale for simple lookups by key. Best when data is naturally nested and read patterns are predictable.

note: The real question is your access pattern: how will you query this data, and how often does the shape change?
caption: Pick based on your actual read/write patterns, not hype. A lot of "NoSQL" problems are really just denormalized SQL problems in disguise.

title: Why your API call is slower than it looks
note: DNS lookup, TCP handshake, then TLS handshake — all happen before your request even reaches the server. HTTP/2 and connection reuse help, but the first request always pays this cost.
caption: A "100ms API" can easily take 300-400ms on a cold connection because of DNS + TCP + TLS setup. Keep-alive and HTTP/2 multiplexing are why reusing connections matters so much.

title: Put the cache header on the right thing
code:
# static assets: cache hard, bust via filename
Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable

# API responses that change often
Cache-Control: no-cache

# user-specific pages
Cache-Control: private, max-age=0
note: immutable only works if the filename changes on every deploy (hashed filenames).
caption: The most common cache-control mistake: caching an HTML page for a year, or never caching a hashed JS bundle at all. Match the header to how often the content actually changes.

title: console.log isn't your only tool
note: All four are built into every browser and Node — no imports needed.
caption: console has more than .log(). table() formats arrays into readable grids, time()/timeEnd() measures duration, and trace() shows you exactly who called this line.

title: Binary search your bug, not just your array
note: git bisect runs a binary search over your commit history. For 1000 commits, that's about 10 tests instead of checking every commit one by one.
caption: When a bug appeared somewhere in the last N commits and you don't know where, don't scroll through history manually. git bisect start, mark a good and bad commit, and it binary-searches for the exact commit that broke it.

title: Clearer git commands you should use
code:
git switch -c feature/login   # new branch
git switch main               # change branch

git restore app.js            # discard edits
git restore --staged app.js   # unstage
note: switch and restore split up the many jobs of git checkout.
caption: git checkout does too many things. switch handles branches and restore handles files, so mistakes are harder to make.

title: Rewrite history without losing work
code:
# squash the last 3 commits into one
git rebase -i HEAD~3

# safer than --force after a rebase:
git push --force-with-lease
note: --force-with-lease fails if someone else pushed in the meantime, unlike plain --force.
caption: Interactive rebase lets you clean up messy commit history before a PR. --force-with-lease protects you from overwriting a teammate's work by accident.

title: Style children on parent hover
code:
Project

View →
note: Mark the parent with group, then use group-hover: on any child.
caption: Hovering a card and changing several elements inside it needs no JavaScript in Tailwind. Just group and group-hover.

title: Where should you store a JWT?

left.label: localStorage
left.body: Easy to use from JS, but readable by any script on the page. A single XSS bug leaks every user's token.

right.label: httpOnly cookie
right.body: Invisible to JavaScript entirely, so XSS can't steal it. Needs CSRF protection since the browser sends it automatically.

note: httpOnly cookies trade an XSS risk for a CSRF risk — but CSRF is far easier to defend against with a SameSite flag and a token.
caption: Storing auth tokens in localStorage is one of the most common security mistakes in frontend apps. httpOnly cookies plus SameSite=Strict close that door.

title: Quick quiz: which request is vulnerable?
question: Your API builds a query like this from user input: `"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + name + "'"`. What's this vulnerable to?
note: Think you know? Answer is in the caption.
caption: Answer: B, SQL injection. String-concatenated SQL lets an attacker pass name = "' OR '1'='1" and return every row. Parameterized queries fix it. Classic one, but still shows up in real codebases through ORMs with a raw-query escape hatch.

title: The habit that actually speeds up PR reviews
note: Reading your own diff top to bottom before requesting review catches typos, leftover console.logs and unclear naming — the stuff reviewers flag that slows everything down.
caption: Reviewers remember who sends clean, self-reviewed PRs versus who sends a first draft every time. A 2-minute self-review before requesting one often saves a full review round-trip.

title: Estimate like a senior, not a hero

left.label: Best case
left.body: "This will take 2 days" assumes no blockers, no surprises, and no context switching. It's almost never what actually happens.

right.label: Realistic estimate
right.body: Add time for review cycles, unknowns in the codebase, and meetings. A senior engineer pads for reality, not optimism.

note: Track your own estimate-vs-actual over a few sprints. Most people are consistently optimistic by a predictable factor — learn yours.
caption: Underestimating isn't a skill gap, it's a habit. The fix is tracking your own estimate accuracy over time and adjusting, not trying to "estimate better" from scratch each time.
